claim: A fruit fly larva has approximately 50,000 cells.
source: even a fruit fly larva has ~50,000 cells
evidence: Cited from Lehner et al., 2001 in the manuscript

claim: A small mammal has more than 1 billion cells.
source: a small mammal has >1 billion cells

claim: The complete cell lineage of Caenorhabditis elegans consists of approximately 1000 cells.
source: its complete lineage (~1000 cells) was deduced by painstaking observation of each cell division under the microscope
evidence: Statement about C. elegans lineage in the introduction

claim: 16 rounds of cell division are required to produce a hatched Drosophila larva.
source: The 16 rounds of cell division required to produce a hatched Drosophila larva, for example, result in about 50,000 cells (Lehner et al., 2001)

claim: The bodies of mice consist of 10^10 cells.
source: The bodies of mice and humans consist of 1010 to 1014 cells respectively (Sender et al., 2016)

claim: The bodies of humans consist of 10^14 cells.
source: The bodies of mice and humans consist of 1010 to 1014 cells respectively (Sender et al., 2016)

claim: Naturally occurring somatic mutations can be used as lineage markers to reconstruct entire cell lineages.
source: Recently it was proposed that naturally occurring somatic mutations, which accumulate in cells during the lifetime of an organism, could be used as lineage markers to reconstruct its entire cell lineage (Frumkin et al., 2005; Salipante and Horwitz, 2006)
evidence: Cited from Frumkin et al., 2005 and Salipante and Horwitz, 2006

claim: The use of naturally occurring somatic mutations for lineage reconstruction is limited by the challenge of detecting rare mutations within individual cell genomes.
source: While this approach is theoretically possible (Frumkin et al., 2005), it is nevertheless limited by the enormous challenge of detecting these rare mutations within the genomes of individual cells
evidence: Statement with citation to Frumkin et al., 2005

claim: CRISPR-induced mutations destroy the match between target and sgRNA, making mutated targets immune to further change.
source: In most cases, the mutation destroys the match between target and sgRNA meaning a mutated target is immune to further change
evidence: Statement about CRISPR mechanism in the introduction

claim: The optimal mutation rate for lineage reconstruction with 100 CRISPR targets after 16 cell divisions is between 0.05 and 0.2 mutations per cell division per target.
source: Mutation rates show a broad optimum between between 0.05 and 0.2 mutations per cell division per target
evidence: Derived from simulation results shown in Figure 2C

claim: Under optimal mutation rates (0.05-0.2), 56-97% of target sites are mutated after 16 cell divisions.
source: under these rates, 56–97% of target sites are mutated after 16 cell divisions

claim: Most CRISPR-induced mutations are small deletions or insertions located close to the Cas9 editing site.
source: As reported in previous studies (van Overbeek et al., 2016; Allen et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018), we found that most of the mutations were located close to the Cas9 editing site

claim: More than 200 distinct mutated states were observed in the FAST target.
source: Focusing on the 9 bp adjacent to the PAM sequence (Figure 4B) we observed >200 mutated states

claim: The frequencies of CRISPR mutations follow an exponential curve, with a few variants occurring at high frequency.
source: The frequencies of mutations follow an exponential curve, with a few variants occurring at high frequency (Figure 4C)
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: 59 mutations account for 95% of the total number of mutations in the FAST target.
source: 59 mutations account for 95% of the total number of mutations

claim: Using the experimentally measured distribution of mutational outcomes, the accuracy of cell lineage reconstruction with 32 FAST targets is 72%.
source: Using the experimentally measured distribution of mutational outcomes, the accuracy of cell lineage reconstruction is 72% (see Figure 5B)

claim: Weighting mutations in inverse proportion to their frequency improves lineage reconstruction accuracy from 72% to 82%.
source: Following this approach, the accuracy of lineage reconstruction using the same 61 states improved from 72% to 82% (Figure 5B)

claim: Early Drosophila embryos initially go through 13 rapid and near-synchronous nuclear divisions to generate a syncytial blastoderm.
source: Early Drosophila embryos, for example, initially go through a series of 13 rapid and near-synchronous nuclear divisions to generate a uniform syncytial blastoderm (Zalokar and Erk, 1976)

claim: The duration of each mitotic cycle in early Drosophila embryos is approximately 10 minutes.
source: during this phase the duration of each mitotic cycle is very short (~10 min)

claim: After cellularisation at cell cycle 14, the rate of cell division in the Drosophila embryo slows considerably and becomes asynchronous.
source: After cellularisation at cell cycle 14, the rate of cell division in the embryo slows considerably and becomes asynchronous (Foe, 1989; Hartenstein, 1993)

claim: With uneven cell division rates approximating Drosophila development, the accuracy of lineage reconstruction using FAST targets falls to 9%.
source: Under these conditions, we would expect the accuracy of lineage reconstruction to be considerably worse, as there will be many fewer mutations accumulated in the rapid early cell cycles, and indeed the accuracy fell to just 9% (without using the weighting scheme; see Figure 5B)

claim: Target dropouts have a major impact on the accuracy of lineage reconstruction.
source: We find that dropouts have a major impact on the accuracy of lineage reconstruction (Figure 6B)

claim: With dropouts, the accuracy of lineage reconstruction using 32 FAST targets drops from 72% to 23%.
source: after 16 cell divisions, the accuracy dropped from 72% to 23% (or from 82% to 26% with weighted mutational outcomes)
evidence: Simulation result comparing scenarios with and without dropouts

claim: The MEMOIR approach using 32 targets with 2 character states achieves only 4% accuracy.
source: We find that the accuracy is only 4%

claim: The optimal mutation rate for lineage reconstruction using SOLiD sequencing (4 character states) lies between 0.05 and 0.12 mutations per cell division.
source: Our results show (Figure 7C) that the optimal mutation rate for lineage reconstruction by this approach lies between 0.05 and 0.12 mutations per cell division

claim: With a single SOLiD read using 32 FAST targets, the mean accuracy of reconstructed cell lineages is 45%.
source: Our results show that, with a single SOLiD read, using a recorder with 32 targets, the mean accuracy of reconstructed cell lineages is 45% (Figure 7B)

claim: The reconstruction accuracy obtained by performing 1 SOLiD sequencing cycle on 64 FAST targets is 69%.
source: We found that the reconstruction accuracy obtained by performing 1 SOLiD sequencing cycle on 64 FAST targets is higher (69%) than performing 2 SOLiD cycles on 32 FAST targets (65%) (Figure 7B)

claim: The reconstruction accuracy obtained by performing 2 SOLiD sequencing cycles on 32 FAST targets is 65%.
source: We found that the reconstruction accuracy obtained by performing 1 SOLiD sequencing cycle on 64 FAST targets is higher (69%) than performing 2 SOLiD cycles on 32 FAST targets (65%) (Figure 7B)

claim: The GESTALT v7 construct contains 10 different CRISPR targets.
source: The v7 construct contains 10 different CRISPR targets that were targeted with 10 different sgRNAs

claim: The estimated mutation rate for GESTALT targets ranges from approximately 0.01 to approximately 0.23 per cell division.
source: The estimated mutation rate ranges from ~0.01 (for target 10) to ~0.23 (for target 7) per cell division

claim: The mean accuracy of the GESTALT approach is 14% after 16 cell divisions.
source: We find that the mean accuracy of the GESTALT approach is just 14% after 16 cell divisions (Figure 6B)

claim: The GESTALT implementation is not suited for reconstructing a complete, accurate cell lineage.
source: This means that this implementation of GESTALT is not suited for reconstructing a complete, accurate cell lineage

claim: Under ideal conditions, 30 targets are sufficient to reach an overall tree accuracy of approximately 70% for a lineage of approximately 65,000 cells.
source: Under ideal conditions (optimized mutation rates, uniform cell divisions, fully sequenced targets), 30 targets are sufficient to reach an overall tree accuracy of ~70% for a lineage of ~65,000 cells

claim: 100 targets would yield trees that have an accuracy above 90% under ideal conditions.
source: 100 targets would yield trees that have an accuracy above 90% (Figure 2D)

claim: More than 200 targets would be required to get a highly accurate (>95%) tree using a single 4-colour SOLiD read per target.
source: If we were only able to take a single 4-colour SOLiD read per target, more than 200 targets would be required to get a highly accurate (>95%) tree (Figure 7C)

claim: Most of the CRISPR recorders published to date rely on at most 10 CRISPR targets.
source: Our analysis suggests that most of the CRISPR recorders published to date, which rely on at most 10 CRISPR targets (McKenna et al., 2016; Raj et al., 2018; Frieda et al., 2017; Junker et al., 2016; Schmidt et al., 2017; Alemany et al., 2018), yield trees of very low overall accuracy and lineage resolution

claim: Most published CRISPR recorders yield trees of very low overall accuracy and lineage resolution.
source: Our analysis suggests that most of the CRISPR recorders published to date, which rely on at most 10 CRISPR targets (McKenna et al., 2016; Raj et al., 2018; Frieda et al., 2017; Junker et al., 2016; Schmidt et al., 2017; Alemany et al., 2018), yield trees of very low overall accuracy and lineage resolution
evidence: Conclusion based on simulation results and comparison with published methods

claim: The clones of 33-64 cells reconstructed in simulations based on the FAST construct without dropouts have a high accuracy of 90%.
source: Our results show, for example, that the clones of 33–64 cells reconstructed in simulations based on our FAST construct without dropouts have a high accuracy of 90% and correspondingly low errors, with less than 5% of both FP and FN
evidence: Simulation result for false positive and false negative analysis

claim: The clones of 33-64 cells reconstructed in simulations based on the FAST construct without dropouts have less than 5% false positives and false negatives.
source: Our results show, for example, that the clones of 33–64 cells reconstructed in simulations based on our FAST construct without dropouts have a high accuracy of 90% and correspondingly low errors, with less than 5% of both FP and FN
evidence: Simulation result for false positive and false negative analysis

claim: The Drosophila U6.2 promoter produces lower levels of CRISPR activity compared to the U6.1 and U6.3 promoters.
source: The Drosophila U6.2 promoter has been shown by previous studies to produce lower levels of CRISPR activity when compared to the U6.1 and U6.3 promoters (Port et al., 2014)

claim: The dinucleotide located 6-7 bp upstream of the PAM is the most informative for lineage reconstruction using SOLiD sequencing.
source: We determined that positions 6–7 bp 5' of the PAM sequence yield the most equiprobable colour frequencies for the FAST target (Figure 7A), minimising homoplasy in the observed character states
evidence: Analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Computer simulations were performed using MATLAB v2017a.
source: Computer simulations were performed using MATLAB v2017a (Mathworks, 2017)

claim: The accuracy of each cell-lineage reconstruction was determined by calculating a measure related to the Robinson-Foulds distance between the reference and inferred trees.
source: The accuracy of each cell-lineage reconstruction was determined by calculating a measure related to the Robinson-Foulds distance between the reference and the inferred trees

claim: Most cell lineages were inferred using the Neighbor-Joining method.
source: Most cell lineages were inferred using the Neighbor-Joining method (NJ)

claim: The Neighbor joining algorithm was implemented using PAUP* software version 4.0a build 158.
source: We used the Neighbor joining algorithm as implemented in the PAUP* software (version 4.0a build 158; (Swofford, 2017))

claim: Accuracy is consistently slightly higher using parsimony compared to Neighbor Joining.
source: We show that, while accuracy is consistently slightly higher using parsimony, the average time taken to reconstruct a tree of only 180 cells is on average ~52 hr compared to less than 1 s using Neighbor Joining (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1)

claim: The average time taken to reconstruct a tree of 180 cells using parsimony is approximately 52 hours.
source: the average time taken to reconstruct a tree of only 180 cells is on average ~52 hr compared to less than 1 s using Neighbor Joining (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1)

claim: The average time taken to reconstruct a tree of 180 cells using Neighbor Joining is less than 1 second.
source: the average time taken to reconstruct a tree of only 180 cells is on average ~52 hr compared to less than 1 s using Neighbor Joining (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1)

claim: The GESTALT data was obtained from zebrafish embryos at 30 hours post-fertilisation.
source: To analyse the accuracy of GESTALT, we used data from the v7 construct at the 30 hr post-fertilisation stage

claim: At 30 hours post-fertilisation, the zebrafish embryo consists of approximately 25,000 cells.
source: At this stage the zebrafish embryo consists of approximately 25,000 cells, resulting from ~15 rounds of cell division

claim: The simulated GESTALT samples produced an average of 3022 alleles.
source: Our simulated samples produced an average of 3022 alleles (s.d. = 877 alleles; see Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Simulation result shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The experimental GESTALT data contained 1,000-2,500 alleles.
source: compared to the 1,000–2,500 alleles found in the experimental data (McKenna et al., 2016)

claim: Rare mutations are better lineage markers than more frequent mutations.
source: Rarely occurring mutations are less likely to appear independently in the same target in more than one branch of the lineage tree (an instance of homoplasy), suggesting that rare mutations are better lineage markers than more frequent mutations

claim: Higher mutation rates are needed for high lineaging accuracy when the rates of cell division are uneven.
source: These results suggest that higher mutation rates are needed for high lineaging accuracy when the rates of cell division are uneven

claim: The problem of dropouts could be reduced by opting for the lower end of the optimal range of mutation rates.
source: The problem of dropouts could be reduced by opting for the lower end of the optimal range of mutation rates; or eliminated by targeting separate loci in the genome rather than arrays of targets
evidence: Proposed solution based on simulation insights

claim: The problem of dropouts could be eliminated by targeting separate loci in the genome rather than arrays of targets.
source: The problem of dropouts could be reduced by opting for the lower end of the optimal range of mutation rates; or eliminated by targeting separate loci in the genome rather than arrays of targets
evidence: Proposed solution based on simulation insights

claim: Optimised recorders will ultimately allow the reconstruction of accurate cell lineages of complex multicellular organisms at the level of a single cell.
source: Our study predicts that optimised recorders will ultimately allow the reconstruction of accurate cell lineages of complex multicellular organisms at the level of a single cell
